summary: Describes a URN namespace for Object Identifiers, letting those dotted numbers be written as URNs. It is informational and replaces RFC 3001.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3061 defines a way to write an Object Identifier as a URN, such as urn:oid:1.3.6.1. It defines the name format but does not define a service that looks up or checks the identifier.

questions: how to write an oid as a urn
what is the oid urn namespace
what characters are allowed in an oid urn
subtitle: A standard way to write Object Identifiers as Uniform Resource Names.

tldr.problem: Object Identifiers are dotted sequences of numbers, and this memo defines how to represent them in the Uniform Resource Name system.
tldr.mechanism: The registered namespace identifier is oid. The name contains the OID digits separated by periods, with no leading zeroes in a number.
tldr.outcome: The form urn:oid:1.3.6.1 names an OID, but RFC 3061 defines no lookup or validation service. It obsoletes RFC 3001.

today: RFC 3061 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 3001. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates this namespace specification.

sections.title: Putting an Object Identifier in a URN
sections.content:
An Object Identifier (OID) is a sequence of numbered branches in a tree. Once an entity receives a branch, it can assign branches below it under the OID rules.

RFC 3061 registers the namespace identifier oid so an OID can be written as a Uniform Resource Name (URN). Examples in the memo include urn:oid:1.3.6.1 and urn:oid:1.3.6.1.4.1.
sections.plainLanguage: An OID is a path of numbers in an identifier tree. Add the urn:oid: prefix to write that path as a URN.

sections.title: The Characters and Number Rules
sections.content:
The part after urn:oid: contains digits from 0 to 9 with periods between numbers. It must not contain a human-readable label, and a number cannot have leading zeroes.

The memo defines lexical equivalence as an exact string match. It does not add any reserved characters to the URN syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: Write only digits with periods between them. Two names match only when their text is exactly the same.

sections.title: Assignment and Resolution
sections.content:
OID assignment rules require each identifier to be unique and not reused. An organization assigned a node can create identifiers below it. The RFC lists the first three branches as assigned to ITU-T, ISO, and joint ISO/ITU-T assignment.

RFC 3061 defines no resolution mechanism and no validation mechanism. A correctly formatted URN therefore does not by itself prove that its OID was assigned or identify a service that can retrieve information about it.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbering authority controls which branches it assigns. This RFC gives no online lookup that confirms who owns a number or retrieves information about it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the namespace introduces no security considerations beyond those already inherent in using OIDs that cannot be verified. It defines a name format, not an authentication or trust mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The name format does not check whether an OID is genuine. Users must not treat the written name as proof of ownership.
